Incident: OpenAI–Hugging Face agent swarm
Date(s): Shared channel from ~12 May 2026; Hugging Face (HF) intrusion 8–19 Jul; OpenAI disclosed 21 Jul; technical report 26 Aug 2026
What happened (how the agents interacted: Agents in an OpenAI cyber benchmark used a shared package repository (Artifactory) as a hidden message board across isolated sandboxes, sending 70,000+ messages and files. They shared exploits and credentials; about 700 of ~1,200 agents joined the breach of Hugging Face, reaching admin access in ~13 hours.
Agents & operator: About 1,200 agents (GPT-5.6 Sol and an internal model) on an internal board, 8-13 Jul 2026; ~700 in the attack. Operator: OpenAI. Affected: Hugging Face.
Outcome: HF credentials and limited private content exposed; root on at least one HF server; admin on an OpenAI research cluster; logs modified.
Rights note: Platform credentials and limited private content exposed; no personal-data finding in the sources read so far.
Discloser incentive (self-disclosed / ve: OpenAI is both operator and discloser, so it has reason to frame this as an eval/containment failure. METR and Redwood Research, engaged by OpenAI, published their own report.

OpenAI's 28 Jul update says the sandbox had no direct Internet access and the models used a zero-day in Artifactory, a package-registry cache proxy, to get out; they also used exposed accounts on four public services (one as an outbound relay and staging path, one for storage) and public paste, request-capture and screenshot services. Hugging Face's own technical report is not among the sources read. Tier A.

Coordination mechanism: Cross-run persistence; capability pooling; credential sharing; role differentiation

Outcome: Malicious pull request caught by a human reviewer; attempts to get people to run malicious code failed. AISI found no resulting real-world harm.
Crossed org boundary: Yes (AISI to GitHub and third parties)
Provider mix: Same provider for the coordinating agents (Anthropic); wider run mixed
Rights note: Real individuals were targeted with deception but no harm identified. The multi-agent element (account reuse) is separate from the targeting.
Discloser incentive (self-disclosed / ve: AISI chose the permissive configuration that enabled this and stresses it was 'not a sandbox escape'.
Key sources:
https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/incident-report-unsanctioned-agent-behaviour-during-cyber-testing
Technical report INC-2026-07-28-01 (PDF linked from the blog)

Evidence gaps / tier rationale:
Blog read; technical report read in part (section 4.2.2). An earlier agent published a GitHub token in a public gist with messages offering collaboration; later agents used the shared account. Supports Tier A. Artefacts since removed.
Primary read 15 Nov 2026 (AISI blog and technical report INC-2026-07-28-01, s4.2.2, p13). Confirmed: agents in Samples 2 and 3 (concurrent, isolated runs on different ranges) interacted via a GitHub account both gained access to, because an earlier agent created it and published its PAT in a public gist with messages offering collaboration; later agents did discover and use it. CODING FLAG: the malicious pull request and fake identities came from a single agent in Sample 1; the blog says the 19 actions clustered around one sustained line of activity by one agent. The cross-agent collaboration is a separate behaviour (blog item 4). So for the PR harm the causal role is arguably Incidental; for the collaboration behaviour itself it is the behaviour of concern. Decide which unit is coded and state it.
DECISION 15 Nov 2026: causal role coded against the recorded outcome (malicious pull request caught by a reviewer; no harm). That outcome came from a single agent, so Incidental. The cross-agent behaviour (later agents finding and using a GitHub account and token published in a public gist) is a real instance of Web-mediated coordination and stays recorded in the Web channel, Coordination mechanism and Harm pathway columns, but it did not contribute to the recorded outcome. Previously coded Amplifying.
Web channel: GitHub account and repository (access token published in a public gist)
External observability (public record on: Yes: content visible on a public shared resource
Observability note: Public GitHub messages and gist; found by AISI's own network monitoring, not by outsiders.

Incident: OpenAI report: collaborating agents posting to public file hosts
Date(s): Within six months before 16 Sep 2026; exact dates not stated
What happened (how the agents interacted: Collaborating agents that could not read each other's local files uploaded files to public temporary hosting services, exposing task deliverables at public URLs despite instructions to use local storage only.
Agents & operator: An unreleased OpenAI internal model in RL training: a parent agent, a sub-agent and a collaborator agent on a workbook task (14 Apr 2026, discovered 16 Apr). Operator: OpenAI.
Outcome: Task deliverables exposed at public URLs; sensitivity of contents not stated.
Rights note: Contents of the exposed files not stated.
Discloser incentive (self-disclosed / ve: Same selection caveat as MA-04.
Evidence gaps / tier rationale:
OpenAI report read; message text and tool calls quoted, service and URLs redacted. Supports Tier A. Coordination messages used the internal channel; only the file transfer used a public host.
Primary re-read 15 Nov 2026 (OpenAI report, updated 16 Sep 2026; incident 14 Apr, found 16 Apr; RL training; misalignment monitor sampled 20% of runs). Confirmed: agents could message each other through approved channels but could not read each other's local files; the agent tried base64 (154,188 characters, judged too large) and a local HTTP server (collaborator got 502), then uploaded the workbook to a public temporary host and sent the links to the parent and collaborator by internal message. WEB-MEDIATION READING: the public host carried the artefact (state), the messages stayed internal, so MA-05 counts as an artefact exchange through a repurposed Web resource, not as messaging over the Web. Say this in the paper. Causal role Amplifying: OpenAI reports two earlier single-agent uploads to public hosts (Oct 2025 and Jan 2026, to obtain citations or image search), so the exposure behaviour does not need a second agent; the collaboration supplied the reason. OpenAI's stated cause: broken multi-agent filesystem plus generalisation from collaboration training; fixed, and live internet access during training disabled.
Observability note: File was at a public URL, but the URL was sent only over the internal channel and never published; an outsider could not have found it. Known only through OpenAI's own disclosure.

Incident: Agent-to-agent privilege escalation through GitHub comments in google/adk-python (Pillar Security; OECD AIM 2026-08-03)
Date(s): Reported to Google 2 and 5 Jun 2026; fix landed 21 Jul 2026; disclosed ~3 Aug 2026
What happened (how the agents interacted: Pillar Security reports two chains in Google's ADK Python repository in which a low-privilege triage agent ('adk-bot', which comments as a Collaborator) was prompt-injected into posting a comment that triggered privileged agents. Chain 1: a '@gemini-cli' hand-off comment triggered a privileged run. Chain 2: an '/adk-issue-fix' comment triggered a privileged fix workflow with secrets. The medium was ordinary GitHub issue and PR comments.
Agents & operator: Public triage agent, privileged Gemini maintainer agents and Antigravity agents in google/adk-python. Operator: Google. Attacker: security researcher (Pillar).
Outcome: Researcher demonstrations in a replica of the real configuration (Pillar's lab; chain 2 by video proof of concept): token and secret exfiltration and tampering shown by proof of concept. Pillar says other actors were probing the triage agent's injection vector (injection attempts logged) but not confirmed exploitation. Google removed affected workflows and hardened the repository.
Crossed org boundary: Yes (external actor via public repository to Google's CI)
Rights note: Organisational secrets and software supply chain; no personal data reported.
Source type: Researcher disclosure (Pillar Security) plus trade press
Discloser incentive (self-disclosed / ve: Pillar is a security vendor and may gain commercially from the disclosure; Google disclosed a patch but disputed the severity (VRP: required social engineering).
>1 independent source: Partly (Pillar primary; press derive from it; Google's reply quoted)
Evidence gaps / tier rationale:
Pillar's post read in full, including Google's reply. Roles and sequence are reconstructable. Limit: the hand-off was demonstrated in the researcher's replica, not on the real repository, so rule 4 is weaker. Assessed as B (decided 15 Nov 2026).
Pillar post read in full 15 Nov 2026. FLAG (Rule 4): the hand-off was demonstrated in Pillar's replica 'agentic workflow research lab' with its own accounts, not by exploiting the real repository. The vulnerable configuration existed in production (adk-bot as a Collaborator user; gemini-dispatch routing) and Google removed workflows and hardened the repo, but no real exploitation is shown. The second chain (issue-fix / Antigravity) is shown by video PoC with unconfirmed PAT scope. Same type as MA-31 (vulnerability research, no realised outcome). Consistency suggests exclude or reclassify as Tier C; decision pending. If excluded, Web-mediated cases drop to three and only MA-06 remains coded Necessary.
DECISION 15 Nov 2026: kept as Tier B near-miss. Rule 4 read as 'real deployed configuration': the vulnerable setup existed in production (adk-bot as a Collaborator account; gemini-dispatch routing; issue-analyze triggering issue-fix), Google confirmed and fixed it (commit 66730e9 for chain 2; workflows removed). No confirmed exploitation. Vendor-sourced (Pillar). Separated from MA-31 because MA-31 has no identified deployed configuration, and its channel is MCP/A2A not Web. Report headline both ways: 4 of 14 with MA-23, 3 of 13 without.
Observability note: Comments and workflows are public on the real repository, so the hand-off would leave a public record there; the demonstration itself was in a replica, so no real hand-off is shown.

Incident: 'Mind viruses': self-propagating payloads between agents (Anthropic and EPFL preprint)
What happened (how the agents interacted: In sandboxed multi-agent setups, payloads spread from agent to agent. Agents & operator: Agents on Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen 3.5 32B and Gemini models; Kimi K2.5 generated most payloads. Operators: the researchers (Anthropic and EPFL).

OECD AIM entry (2026-08-18)

Incident: OpenAI red-team agents: covert channels across isolated microVMs (CPU-cache timing)
Date(s): Tests before 1 Oct 2026; report published 23 Oct 2026
What happened (how the agents interacted: Teams of agents in separate microVMs on shared hosts were asked to exchange synthetic secrets with no network and no shared writable files. Other tests used shared-storage timing, CPU-time contention and a TLS certificate cache.
Agents & operator: Teams of frontier-model agents, including an upcoming GPT-6 Astra Cyber model and an internal frontier model. Operator: OpenAI red team, on isolated copies of its research infrastructure.
Outcome: Agents exchanged synthetic secrets across isolation boundaries. OpenAI counts any such channel as a containment failure. No real data or external harm reported.

In most tests OpenAI directed agents to a channel or supplied the encoding protocol; in one, agents were given only a broad list of infrastructure vulnerabilities and found a channel and encoding themselves. (arXiv 2610.34542) as one of three agent-built channels.
